text.en: Children sit in a circle and count from 1. Whoever gets a multiple of 3 says idli instead of the number, whoever gets a multiple of 5 says vada, and whoever gets a number that is both says idli-vada. Who says idli-vada first? The answer is 15. This simple game hides big ideas: common multiples, common factors, prime numbers, and the surprising fact that every number is built from primes in only one way.

In the idli-vada game, idli is said at 3, 6, 9, 12 and so on, and vada at 5, 10, 15 and so on. The numbers that are multiples of both 3 and 5 are called common multiples, and the first of them is 15. From 1 to 90, idli (including idli-vada) is said 30 times, vada 18 times, and idli-vada 6 times, at 15, 30, 45, 60, 75 and 90. The tenth idli-vada comes at 150. Every common multiple of 3 and 5 is a multiple of 15. If the game is played to 900, idli-vada is said 60 times, vada 180 times and idli is said 300 times. In the Jump Jackpot game, Grumpy hides a treasure on a number, and Jumpy jumps in equal steps from 0 to reach it. He lands on the treasure only if the jump size is a factor of that number.
A number is a factor of another if it divides it exactly. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. Each pair of factors multiplies to give 12, such as 3 x 4. Common factors are the factors shared by two numbers. The common factors of 20 and 28 are 1, 2 and 4, and those of 35 and 50 are 1 and 5. Guna wants to arrange 12 figs in a rectangle and he can do it in several ways because 12 has several factors. Anshu has 7 figs and can only make a single row, because 7 has only the factors 1 and 7.
A number with exactly two factors, 1 and itself, is called a prime number. The first primes are 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19. A number with more than two factors is called a composite number, for example 4, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 12. The number 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite. The number 2 is the only even prime, because every other even number is divisible by 2 and so has at least three factors. Between 21 and 30 there are 2 primes, 23 and 29, and 8 composite numbers. The Sieve of Eratosthenes finds primes. Cross out 1, circle 2 and cross out its multiples, circle the next uncrossed number 3 and cross out its multiples, and continue. The circled numbers are the primes, and there are 25 of them up to 100.
Two numbers are called co-prime if they have no common factor other than 1. In the treasure game with two treasures, a pair is safe from Jumpy only if the numbers are co-prime. The pair 12 and 26 is not safe, because a jump of 2 reaches both. The pair 4 and 9 is safe. Among 15 and 39, 4 and 15, 18 and 29, and 20 and 55, the safe pairs are 4 and 15, and 18 and 29. Two distinct primes are always co-prime, and a prime and any positive whole number that it does not divide are co-prime. Two positive even numbers are never co-prime, as both are divisible by 2.
Anshu wrote 56 = 14 x 4 and 63 = 21 x 3 and claimed there is no common factor, so they are co-prime. But Guna wrote 56 = 7 x 8 and 63 = 9 x 7 and found the common factor 7. A single factorisation does not list all the factors. A reliable method is prime factorisation: keep breaking composite factors until only primes are left. For 56 we get 56 = 4 x 14 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 7. Each prime in it is called a prime factor. Every number greater than 1 has a prime factorisation. A prime is its own factorisation, and 1 has none. For 36 we can start from 2 x 18, 3 x 12, 4 x 9 or 6 x 6 and always end with two 2s and two 3s. There is only one prime factorisation of a number, apart from the order of the factors. This is why 30 = 2 x 3 x 5 whichever order we multiply in. With prime factorisations, co-prime checking is easy. 56 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 7 and 63 = 3 x 3 x 7 share the prime 7, so they are not co-prime, while 80 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 5 and 63 = 3 x 3 x 7 share none, so they are co-prime.
We can check divisibility without long division. A number is divisible by 10 if it ends in 0, by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5, and by 2 if it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. So 8560 is divisible by 10, 5 and 2. For 4 the last digit is not enough, since 12 is a multiple of 4 but 22 is not. Instead look at the last two digits: a number is divisible by 4 if the number formed by its last two digits is. So 8536 is divisible by 4 because 36 is. For 8 look at the last three digits. 8536 is divisible by 8 because 536 = 8 x 67, and 8560 is divisible by 8 because 560 = 8 x 70. The reason is that 100 is a multiple of 4 and 1000 is a multiple of 8, so only the last few digits can affect divisibility. Tests for 3, 6, 7 and 9 come in later classes.
Leap years show divisibility at work. A year is a leap year if it is a multiple of 4, except century years, which must be multiples of 400. So 2024 is a leap year, and 2100 is not. In a prime puzzle grid you fill the cells with primes so that each row product and column product match the given numbers, which is a nice use of prime factorisation. A perfect number equals the sum of its factors other than itself. The factors of 6 are 1, 2 and 3, which add to 6, so 6 is the smallest perfect number, and 28 is the next one.

text.en: Compare 7,264 and 7,268. Both pass the test for divisibility by four because 64 and 68 are multiples of four. Will both pass the test for divisibility by eight?
For divisibility by eight, use the last three digits. Two hundred sixty-four is eight times thirty-three. Two hundred sixty-eight is four more, so only 7,264 is divisible by eight.
Eight and nine are both composite, yet their only common factor is one. Eight uses only twos as prime factors, and nine uses only threes. Co-prime numbers can both be composite.

problem.en: Write the prime factorisation of 84 and tell whether 84 and 55 are co-prime.

text.en: Break 84 = 4 x 21 = 2 x 2 x 3 x 7.

why.en: Keep splitting until only primes are left.

text.en: Break 55 = 5 x 11.
84 has primes 2, 3, 7 and 55 has primes 5, 11, so there is no common prime and the numbers are co-prime.

why.en: Numbers with no common prime factor are co-prime.

problem.en: Is 56 co-prime to 63? Check by prime factorisation, and explain why 56 = 14 x 4 and 63 = 21 x 3 is not a good check.

text.en: Both have the prime 7, so 7 is a common factor and the numbers are not co-prime.

why.en: A common prime factor means they are not co-prime.

text.en: 14 x 4 and 21 x 3 only show some factors, so we cannot be sure there is no common factor.

why.en: Only a complete prime factorisation shows all the factors.

problem.en: Is 8536 divisible by 4 and by 8? Is 8560 divisible by 4, 5 and 8?

text.en: For 4 look at the last two digits: 36 is divisible by 4, so 8536 is divisible by 4.

why.en: The last two digits decide divisibility by 4.

text.en: For 8 look at the last three digits: 536 = 8 x 67, so 8536 is divisible by 8.

why.en: The last three digits decide divisibility by 8.

text.en: For 8560: 60 is divisible by 4, the last digit 0 means divisible by 5, and 560 = 8 x 70 means divisible by 8.

why.en: Use the test for each number in turn.

problem.en: Find the number whose prime factorisation has one 2, two 3s and one 11.

text.en: Write the product 2 x 3 x 3 x 11.

why.en: Use each prime as many times as given.

prompt.en: Explain how to check if two numbers are co-prime and why prime factorisation helps.

requiredIdeas.en: Co-prime numbers have no common factor other than 1.
Write the prime factorisation of each number.
If no prime appears in both, the numbers are co-prime; otherwise they are not.
One single factorisation can miss common factors, so we need the complete prime factorisation.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking that two numbers are co-prime because they look different in a single factorisation.
Believing all odd numbers are prime, for example 9 and 15 are not.
Using the last digit to test divisibility by 4.

points.en: A common multiple is a multiple of two numbers, and a common factor divides both.
A prime has exactly two factors; a composite has more than two; 1 is neither.
The Sieve of Eratosthenes lists primes; there are 25 primes up to 100.
Co-prime numbers share no factor other than 1.
Every number greater than 1 has exactly one prime factorisation, apart from the order.
Divisibility tests: 2, 5 and 10 by the last digit, 4 by the last two digits, 8 by the last three digits.
